food.text: The Yamnaya of the steppe lived mostly on animal husbandry, fishing and foraging. Isotope studies of people from the Dnieper Valley suggest a diet based on land animals, with almost no contribution from freshwater or aquatic resources.
Archaeologist Anthony speculates that the Yamnaya ate meat, milk, yogurt, cheese, and soups made from seeds and wild vegetables. They also probably drank mead.

The Catacomb culture of the Pontic steppe relied mostly on stockbreeding, with remains of cattle, sheep, goat, horse and some pigs. Plant remains are exceedingly rare, yet traces of wheat such as einkorn and emmer have been found.
The Abashevo culture of the middle Volga and southern Urals had a mixed agricultural economy. People kept cattle, sheep, pigs and goats, and stone grinders and metal sickles are evidence of farming.

Abashevo cattle were of the Ukrainian Grey type. This breed had earlier been raised by Neolithic cultures of the Pontic steppe and along the Danube, and the Sintashta and Srubnaya cultures later adopted it.

Srubnaya settlements have yielded bronze sickles, grinding stones, and the remains of domestic cattle, sheep and pigs. These finds indicate that the Srubnaya practiced both agriculture and stockbreeding.
Sintashta settlements held between 200 and 700 people. Their economies heavily exploited domesticated cattle, sheep and goats alongside horses, with occasional hunting of wild fauna.

Wooden ploughs have been found at Catacomb burials, indicating that agriculture was practiced even in a herding culture. Animal sacrifices, including the head and hooves of goats, sheep, horses and cattle, occur in about 16% of Catacomb graves, and cattle sacrifices were more frequent among the Catacomb people than among the Yamnaya.

The Fatyanovo culture is viewed as introducing an economy based on domestic livestock into the forest zone of Russia. Its animals included sheep, cattle, horse and dog. The presence of domestic swine suggests the society was not fully mobile.
The Cucuteni–Trypillia people grew wheat, rye and peas and harvested them with scythes made of flint-inlaid blades. The grain was milled into flour by quern-stones.

art.text: Kurgan stelae are anthropomorphic stone slabs, images cut from stone, set atop, within or around burial mounds called kurgans. They were probably memorials to the honoured dead. The earliest are associated with the Pit Grave culture of the Pontic-Caspian steppe.

Kurgan stelae were carved over more than three millennia by many different cultures. The earliest belong to the Pit Grave culture, Iron Age examples are identified with the Scythians, and medieval ones with Turkic peoples. They are found in large numbers in Southern Russia and Ukraine, among other places.

Bronze Age artisans in the lands of modern Ukraine made armlets, hairpins, pendants and fibulae. Many earlier cultures there, including the Corded Ware, Globular Amphora and Yamna cultures, were already advanced in metal craft techniques.

Arkaim is a fortified Sintashta site in the Southern Urals, now dated to about 2050 to 1900 BC. Scholars have read its layout as a city "reproducing the model of the universe" described in the ancient Indo-Aryan and Iranian spiritual literature of the Vedas and the Avesta.

The earliest anthropomorphic stelae are associated with the early Bronze Age Yamna Horizon, in particular the Kemi Oba culture of Crimea and the adjacent steppe. Around three hundred survive in Ukraine, most of them very crude stone slabs. Each has a simple protruding head and a few features such as eyes or breasts carved into the stone.

Arkaim has three concentric rings of walls and three radial streets. This layout may reflect the city of King Yama described in the Rigveda. Its foundation walls and the dwellings of the second ring follow what some researchers have described as swastika-like patterns.

About twenty of the stelae found in Ukraine are known as statue menhirs, and they are far more complex than the crude slabs. They feature ornaments, weapons, and human or animal figures, turning a simple marker into a carved scene.

Copper production workshops have been found at archaeological sites of the Yamna culture in Ukraine. Forging, lost-wax casting, and casting in forms became common techniques among the metalworkers of these early cultures.

war.text: The Sintashta culture of the Southern Urals was marked by high levels of militarism and extensive fortified settlements, of which 23 are known. The earlier Abashevo culture had already been marked by endemic intertribal warfare, and in the Sintashta period ecological stress and competition for resources intensified it. This drove fortification on an unprecedented scale and innovations such as the war chariot. Many Sintashta graves were furnished with weapons.

The earliest known chariots have been found in Sintashta burials. The culture is considered a strong candidate for the origin of the technology, which spread throughout the Old World and played an important role in ancient warfare.

The Catacomb culture buried its dead with weapons such as stone and metal axes, arrows, daggers and maces. Its people also included craft specialists, among them bronze workers and weapons manufacturers.

At Sintashta, the largest of five cemeteries held forty graves. Some were chariot burials, producing the oldest known chariots in the world. Others contained horse sacrifices, up to eight horses killed in a single grave, along with stone, copper and bronze weapons and silver and gold ornaments. It has been suggested that these funerary sacrifices strongly resemble the funerary rituals described in the Rig Veda.
Sintashta itself was a fortified settlement dating to about 2100 to 1800 BC, in what is now Chelyabinsk Oblast, Russia. It has been characterised as a "fortified metallurgical industrial center."
On the island of Bayda in the Dnieper river, archaeologists found a stone-built fortress of the late Catacomb period. It was surrounded by a ditch.

Almost a third of Poltavka skulls show signs of wounds, often mortal, and 80 percent of Poltavka graves contain males. Poltavka burials also hold an increased presence of ornaments and weapons, which is interpreted as evidence of increased social stratification. One burial in the Volga region is notable for containing a large copper club.

The Poltavka culture shared many traits with the contemporaneous Sintashta culture, including similar weapons, horse sacrifices and chariot-driving gear. Horse burials were a custom the Poltavka people inherited from the Yamnaya culture, the Khvalynsk culture and Samara culture. Sintashta builders often put new settlements on top of earlier Poltavka ones.

The Abashevo culture, found in the middle Volga and Kama valleys and dated to about 2200 to 1850 BC, is notable for its metallurgy and for evidence of chariot use in its end phase. Archaeological evidence suggests its society was intensely warlike: mass graves reveal inter-tribal battles involving hundreds of warriors on both sides, and a well-known kurgan at Pepkino held the remains of twenty-eight males who appear to have died violent deaths. High-status graves contained weapons along with silver and copper ornaments.

A chariot burial at Krivoye Lake was dated by Anthony and Vinogradov to around 2000 BC. This is early enough to challenge scholars who argued that the Andronovo culture was too late to be linked to chariot-using Aryans, who appear in Mitanni by the 15th century BC.
A knife ascribed to the Catacomb culture in the Donets, dated to about 2500 BC, had a handle of arsenical bronze and a blade made of iron.

literature.text: Linguists reconstructing the Proto-Indo-European language, which mainstream scholars place on the Pontic-Caspian steppe, have found traces of oral heroic poetry or song lyrics. It used stock phrases such as "imperishable fame" and "the wheel of the sun". No written record of this language has been found.

The Stone Tomb, Kamyana Mohyla, in Ukraine is a group of sandstone blocks with petroglyphs inside its caves and grottoes. Archaeologist Valentin Danylenko claimed to have found thirty caves with petroglyph inscriptions dated from the 20th century BC to the 17th century AD.

Arkaim, a fortified Bronze Age site in the Southern Urals, was built by the Sintashta culture. Scholars have read its layout as a city "reproducing the model of the universe" described in ancient Indo-Aryan and Iranian spiritual literature, the Vedas and the Avesta.

The Proto-Indo-Europeans lived in preliterate societies, so their myths are not directly recorded. Scholars of comparative mythology rebuild them by comparing similar stories found in the languages descended from Proto-Indo-European.

Nearly all Indo-European mythologies share a story in which a thunder-god or a hero associated with thunder slays a serpent or dragon, often multi-headed and called a "blocker of waters". The thunder-god smashes its many heads in an epic battle, releasing the torrents of water it had pent up. The serpent loses in every version, though in some, such as the Norse Ragnarök myth, the hero or god dies together with his enemy.

Arkaim has three concentric rings of walls and three radial streets. This plan possibly reflects the city of King Yama described in the Rigveda, a link between an excavated Urals settlement and an ancient hymn collection.

In the reconstructed story, the cattle that the gods gave *Trito were stolen by a three-headed serpent, *Ngʷhi, and *Trito first suffers at its hands before overcoming it, fortified by an intoxicating drink and aided by the Sky-Father. That story served as a model for later cattle-raiding epic myths and most likely as a moral justification for raiding among Indo-European peoples. In the original legend, *Trito only takes back what rightfully belongs to his people, those who sacrifice properly to the gods.

science.text: The Yamnaya culture of the Pontic–Caspian steppe, dated to 3300–2600 BC, used two-wheeled carts and four-wheeled wagons. These vehicles are thought to have been drawn by oxen at this time. The Yamnaya people were nomads or semi-nomads.

It has been suggested that Seima-Turbino people spread across a frontier of some 4,000 miles in just five to six generations. This migration supposedly enabled people from Finland in the west to Thailand in the east to use the same metal working technology. In some areas they also shared horse breeding and riding.

It has been conjectured that changes in climate around 2000 BCE, and the ecological, economic and political changes that followed, triggered a rapid migration of Seima-Turbino people. They moved westward into northeast Europe, eastward into Korea, and southward into Southeast Asia.

Several Yamnaya skeletons show characteristics in their bone morphology that may have been caused by long-term horseriding. This is part of the evidence that these steppe people rode horses. The Yamnaya culture also used carts and wagons.

The archaeozoologist William T. Taylor disputes the evidence for Yamnaya horseriding, arguing that horse domestication long postdates the Yamnaya culture. Recent genetic studies indicate that horse domestication in Eurasia happened after c. 2700 BC.

The Seima-Turbino culture is named after the Seyma cemetery, near the confluence of the Oka and Volga rivers, first excavated around 1914. It is also named after the Turbino cemetery in Perm, first excavated in 1924.

politics.text: The Sintashta culture, dated to c. 2200-1900 BCE, is widely regarded as the origin of the Indo-Iranian languages. Its people built extensive fortified settlements, 23 of which are known, and the earliest known chariots come from their burials.

The Sintashta culture of the Southern Urals, dated to c. 2200–1900 BCE, was marked by high levels of militarism. The preceding Abashevo culture had already been marked by endemic intertribal warfare, and ecological stress and competition for resources intensified it in the Sintashta period. This drove the construction of fortifications on an unprecedented scale, of which 23 settlements are known, and the invention of the war chariot.

The Yamnaya culture, dated to 3300–2600 BC, was succeeded in the west by the Catacomb culture and in the east by the Poltavka culture on the middle Volga. Both were in turn followed by the Srubnaya culture, which lasted from the 18th to the 12th century BC.

In the early 2nd millennium BC, the Lola culture of the North Caucasus came under increasing pressure from the Srubnaya culture, which was advancing from the Middle Volga region. By 1800 BC, the Srubnaya had replaced the Lola population.

The Fatyanovo culture developed around 2900 BC, probably as a result of a mass migration of Corded Ware peoples from Central Europe. It expanded eastwards at the expense of the Volosovo culture of indigenous forest foragers, which disappeared when the Fatyanovo people pushed into the Upper and Middle Volga basin. The Balanovo branch coexisted with the Volosovo people at some sites and also displaced them, while a genetic study found the Fatyanovo people were substantially different from the Volosovo and do not appear to have mixed with them. The Fatyanovo people also developed copper mines in the western Urals.
The Catacomb culture flourished on the Pontic steppe in 2,500–1,950 BC as an outgrowth of the Yamnaya culture. Its influences have been suggested to be found as far away as Italy, Greece, and Syria.

More than twenty other structures built to patterns similar to Arkaim have been found across an area spanning the southern Urals to the north of Kazakhstan. Together they form the so-called Land of Towns.

The Sintashta site in Chelyabinsk Oblast is the remains of a fortified settlement, mostly occupied around 2100–1800 BC, with rectangular houses arranged in a circle 140 m across and ringed by a timber-reinforced earthen wall, gate towers and a deep ditch. It has been characterised as a "fortified metallurgical industrial center," with copper and bronze metalworking in every house excavated. Its five cemeteries include chariot burials, the oldest known chariots in the world, and graves holding horse sacrifices, up to eight in a single grave, alongside weapons and silver and gold ornaments.

Over two hundred settlements of the Abashevo culture have been found, yet just two of them appear to have been fortified. Even so, archaeological evidence suggests Abashevo society was intensely warlike: mass graves reveal inter-tribal battles involving hundreds of warriors on both sides, and a well-known kurgan at Pepkino held the remains of twenty-eight males who appear to have died violent deaths. The culture, dated c. 2200–1850 BC, played a major role in the development of the Sintashta and Srubnaya cultures, and warfare appears to have been more frequent in its late period.
The Lola culture emerged in the North Caucasus c. 2200 BC as a result of migrations of peoples from the east Caucasus. It replaced the local variants of the Catacomb culture.

The Poltavka culture lasted until 2200–2100 BCE and marked the transition from the Yamnaya culture to the Srubnaya culture. Genetic studies suggest that its end is associated with major population changes.

philosophy.text: Arkaim, a fortified Bronze Age site in the Southern Urals, has three concentric rings of walls and three radial streets. Scholars have read this layout as a city "reproducing the model of the universe" described in ancient Indo-Aryan and Iranian spiritual literature, the Vedas and the Avesta.

Proto-Indo-Iranian religion, generally associated with the Sintashta culture (2050-1900 BCE), included the universal force *Hṛta-, known as rta in Sanskrit and asha in Avestan. It also featured the sacred drink *sawHma- (Soma in Sanskrit, Haoma in Avestan) and gods of social order such as *mitra-.

Some scholars think Arkaim's concentric design reflects the city of King Yima, described as the first Indo-Iranian Priest king in ancient religious literature. The structure may also echo the city of King Yama in the Rigveda.

The discovery of Arkaim and the Land of Towns has fueled schools of thought among Russian Rodnovers, Roerichians, Zoroastrians, Hindus and others. They regard the site as the second homeland of the Indo-Europeans, and some claim all Vedic knowledge originated in the southern Urals.

The Rigveda records an early stage of Vedic religion and has strong linguistic and cultural similarities with the early Iranian Avesta. These similarities derive from Proto-Indo-Iranian times, often associated with the early Andronovo culture of c. 2000 BCE.

The earliest kurgan stelae, anthropomorphic stone images set atop or around burial mounds, are associated with the Pit Grave culture of the Pontic-Caspian steppe. Under the mainstream Kurgan hypothesis, that links them to the Proto-Indo-Europeans.

Arkaim, a fortified Sintashta site in the Southern Urals, has three concentric rings of walls and three radial streets. Some scholars think its layout may reflect the city of King Yama described in the Rigveda.

The foundation walls and dwellings of Arkaim's second ring follow what some researchers call 'swastika-like patterns'. The same symbol appears on various artifacts from the site, which belongs to the Sintashta culture.

In the Avesta, Ahura Mazda upholds asha, the cosmic moral order. The Vedic Varuna, most powerful of the Asuras, shares traits with him, including a role as king among lesser gods and arbiter of law and morality among mortals. Varuna and the Asuras uphold the analogous concept of rta.

The Russian Zoroastrian movement identifies Arkaim as the place where Zoroaster was born. Some others identify it as the Asgard of Odin from Germanic mythology. Arkaim is designated a "national and spiritual shrine" of Russia and is a holy site for Rodnover, Zoroastrian and other religious movements.

The Sanskrit word 'deva' is linguistically related to the Avestan 'daeva'. Yet Indra, the greatest of the devas in Vedic literature, is listed in Zoroastrian texts as one of the greatest evil forces, sometimes second only to Angra Mainyu. Rejecting the daevas is a key mark of a Zoroastrian follower.

culture.text: The Yamnaya culture of the steppe between the Southern Bug, Dniester and Ural rivers, dated 3300 to 2600 BC, takes its name from its burial tradition. Yamnaya is a Russian word meaning 'related to pits', because these people buried their dead in tumuli, called kurgans, containing simple pit chambers. The bodies were laid on their backs with bent knees and covered in ochre, and the graves were often accompanied by animal offerings. In some areas elite individuals were buried with complete wooden wagons.

The Yamnaya economy was based on animal husbandry, fishing and foraging, along with the manufacture of ceramics, tools and weapons. The people were nomads or semi-nomads, and their society was organised as a chiefdom.

The Fatyanovo culture is viewed as introducing an economy based on domestic livestock into the forest zone of Russia. The animals were sheep, cattle, horse and dog, and domestic swine are also found, which suggests a society that was not entirely mobile.

The earliest known chariots have been found in Sintashta burials in the Southern Urals, in a culture dated c. 2200–1900 BCE. Sintashta people also carried out intense copper mining and bronze metallurgy, and 23 of their fortified settlements are known.

The Yamnaya culture used two-wheeled carts and four-wheeled wagons, which are thought to have been drawn by oxen at this time. Some Yamnaya skeletons show bone changes that may have been caused by long-term horseriding, though the archaeozoologist William T. Taylor disputes this evidence.

Archaeologists point to flexed burial under barrows, battle-axes and ceramics as evidence that the Fatyanovo culture was brought by newcomers. It has been described as a 'genuine folk movement' from Central Europe into the forests of Russia.

Expanding eastwards, the Fatyanovo people developed copper mines in the western Urals. From 2300 BC they established settlements engaged in bronze metallurgy, giving rise to the Balanovo culture, which contributed to the Abashevo culture, in turn contributing to the Sintashta culture.

Several Sintashta towns were built over older Poltavka settlements or close to Poltavka cemeteries. Poltavka motifs are common on Sintashta pottery, showing how the earlier steppe culture lived on in Sintashta daily life.

Horses buried in Sintashta kurgans together with the earliest spoke-wheeled chariots, around 2000–1800 BC, all carried the DOM2 genetic profile. This profile later spread across Asia at the same time as chariotry and Indo-Iranian languages.
